title: One blocked square: how many routes?
hook: Listing every robot route gets out of hand fast. Can you count them without listing?

knows: memoization means reusing answers already computed (fib-call-explosion)
doesNotKnow: that the routes into a grid cell equal the routes into its left and upper neighbours added together

misconception: To count robot routes you must list every route; a blocked cell means redoing the work.
objective: The learner can fill a 4 x 4 grid with left-plus-above counts, with the blocked cell at 0, get 8 at the corner, and explain why each cell is the sum of its two neighbours.

claims.text: On a 4 x 4 grid, moving only right or down, with the cell in row 2, column 2 blocked, there are 8 routes from top-left to bottom-right.
claims.source: Demo.tsx counts(true) corner = 8; builder re-ran the same fill in Node: [[1,1,1,1],[1,0,1,2],[1,1,2,4],[1,2,4,8]]. Cross-check: 20 − 12 = 8.

claims.text: With the block removed the corner reads 20: the block cut 12 routes.
claims.source: Demo.tsx counts(false) corner = 20 = C(6,3). Routes through (2,2): 2 to reach it x C(4,2) = 6 from it = 12.

claims.text: Every route into a cell arrives from the left or from above, so its count is those two added; a blocked cell holds 0; each edge cell has only one way in, so it holds 1 route.
claims.source: The last move into (r, c) is either right from (r, c−1) or down from (r−1, c); these route sets are disjoint, so N(r,c) = N(r,c−1) + N(r−1,c). A blocked cell has no routes into it. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): node DP grid [[1,1,1,1],[1,0,1,2],[1,1,2,4],[1,2,4,8]] = brute force over all 20 paths (8 avoid the block; 20 open). Disjoint last move gives N(r,c) = N(r,c-1) + N(r-1,c). Note: 'edge cell' means the top row and left column (the stage fills those as one edge, message 'Edge cells have only one way in'); bottom and right border cells have two ways in. Wording suggestion (non-blocking): 'each top-row or left-column cell'.

claims.text: Reusing counts you already have, instead of listing routes one by one, is called dynamic programming.
claims.source: CLRS (3rd ed.) ch. 15 introduction: dynamic programming solves each subproblem once and stores its answer. Bellman, Dynamic Programming, 1957.
Base case N(1,1) = 1 (the empty route), standard for lattice-path counting.

recall.question: Moving only right or down, a cell's left neighbour has 3 routes into it and the cell above has 6. How many routes reach the cell?
recall.why: Every route arrives from the left or from above, never both, so the counts add: 3 + 6 = 9.
